terms.definition: A heuristic that never overestimates the true remaining cost, so A* is guaranteed to find the cheapest path.
A precise sequence of steps for solving a problem or completing a task.
A route-finding method copied from ants: good paths get reinforced by virtual pheromone, weak ones fade.
The smallest unit of an element that still has that element’s chemical properties.
How quickly a compressor reacts once the signal rises above the threshold, usually measured in milliseconds.
An automatic volume control that turns a sound down when it gets louder than a set threshold, narrowing the gap between loud and quiet parts.
A compressor with a very high ratio and very fast attack that keeps a signal from ever exceeding a set ceiling.
Going back to the last choice point after hitting a dead end, then trying another way.
The variety of living things in an area, including differences among species, genes, and ecosystems.
The number of legal moves available from a given position. Higher branching factors make games harder for AI to calculate fully.
A search that checks all cells one step away, then two steps away, and so on. It finds the fewest-steps path.
A substance that speeds up a chemical reaction without being used up by the reaction.
Distortion that happens when a signal goes above the maximum level a system can handle, flattening the tops of the waveform.
In a search, the cells already checked. The search won't expand them again.
A number that multiplies a variable or quantity, such as 3 in 3x.
How strongly a compressor reduces sound above the threshold; at 4:1, every 4 dB of input over the threshold comes out as 1 dB.
The bend in a compressor's transfer curve at the threshold; a soft knee eases compression in gradually, a hard knee starts it abruptly.
The level, in decibels, above which a compressor starts turning the sound down.
A number in an ordered set that identifies a point’s position on a grid or in space.
A system of government in which people have the power to choose leaders and influence decisions.
How many turns ahead an AI calculates. A depth of 1 looks only at the immediate next move.
A search that follows one path as far as it can, then backtracks at dead ends. It finds a path, not the best one.
A search that always expands the cheapest-so-far node, guaranteeing the lowest-cost path when costs aren't negative.
The difference, in decibels, between the quietest and loudest parts of a sound or system.
A community of living things interacting with one another and with their physical environment.
The cost of crossing an edge or entering a tile. In the rover lab, open ground costs 1 and sand costs 3.
The capacity to cause change or do work, such as moving, heating, or lighting something.
The study of a word’s origin and how its form and meaning have changed over time.
Straight-line (“as the crow flies”) distance between two points.
Marking every cell connected to a starting cell, like an image editor's paint-bucket tool.
A push or pull that can change an object’s motion or shape.
In a search, the cells found but not checked yet (also called the open set). The waiting cells in the lab.
A rule that assigns exactly one output to each allowed input.
How many decibels a compressor or limiter is turning the signal down at a given moment.
A vast, branching mathematical map of every possible future sequence of moves.
The branch of mathematics that studies shapes, sizes, positions, and spaces.
In computer science, a set of nodes (places) joined by edges (connections).
A connection between two nodes in a graph. It can be one-way (directed) or two-way (undirected).
A search that always expands whichever cell looks closest to the goal, ignoring the cost paid so far.
The time required for half of the unstable nuclei in a sample to decay.
A quick, educated guess used to guide a search; in A*, an estimate of the cost left to reach the goal.
A testable explanation or prediction based on observations and prior knowledge.
A form of an element whose atoms have the same number of protons but a different number of neutrons.
One repeated cycle of a process, often used to test and improve a design or solution.
Gain added after compression to restore the overall level lost when the loud parts were turned down.
Horizontal steps plus vertical steps, like walking city blocks. It fits grids with no diagonal moves.
A figure of speech that describes one thing as another to suggest a meaningful comparison.
A decision rule used in artificial intelligence and game theory for minimizing the possible loss for a worst case scenario.
Two or more atoms held together by chemical bonds as a single unit.
Connected walkable polygons laid over a 3D game level, searched in place of a fine grid.
A single point in a graph or tree, like one cell on a map, one city on a route, or one board state in a game tree.
The cheapest possible route. BFS finds the fewest steps; Dijkstra and A* find the lowest total cost.
Finding a route between two points through a space with obstacles, costs, or rules.
A point of view; in art, a method for showing depth and three-dimensional space on a flat surface.
The process plants, algae, and some bacteria use to turn light energy, water, and carbon dioxide into sugars.
Original evidence created during the time being studied, such as a letter, photograph, artifact, or firsthand account.
A to-do list that always hands back the lowest-scored item first. Dijkstra and A* both use one.
An early model built to test an idea, reveal problems, and guide improvements.
An optimization technique that skips evaluating branches of the game tree if the AI has already found a provably better move elsewhere.
A comparison of two quantities by division, often written with a colon or as a fraction.
A programming technique where a function repeatedly calls itself to break down complex problems into simpler ones.
How quickly a compressor stops reducing gain after the signal falls back below the threshold.
To generate a final image, animation, or view from digital scene data or code.
Running the search again when the map changes, like a map app rerouting around traffic.
A pattern of sounds and silences organized through time.
A compressor input that lets a different signal control the gain reduction, such as ducking music under a voice.
The speed of a piece of music, usually measured in beats per minute.
An end-game scenario (win, loss, or draw) where the game tree stops growing and is assigned a fixed score.
A symbol or named value that can represent different numbers, measurements, or data.
Simultaneous Localization And Mapping: a robot builds a map of an unknown place while using that same map to track where it is.
Figuring out where a robot is (and which way it faces) by comparing what its sensors see with a map.
Light Detection and Ranging: a sensor that times reflected laser pulses to measure distances, often spinning to scan a full circle.
Estimating how far and which way a robot has moved by counting wheel turns and measuring rotation. Small errors add up over time (drift).
A robot map that splits space into cells, each storing the probability that the cell is blocked by an obstacle.
An estimation method that tracks many random guesses (particles), scores each against sensor data, and resamples the best ones.
RRT: a motion planner that grows a tree of short branches toward randomly sampled points until one reaches the goal. RRT* also shortens the path over time.
A reactive robot planner where the goal attracts the robot and obstacles repel it, and the robot follows the combined force.
DWA: a local planner that tests the speeds and turn rates a robot can reach in the next instant, predicts each arc, and picks the safest one heading toward the goal.
A robot drive with two independently powered wheels and no steering; it turns by spinning one wheel faster than the other.
The math of motion — positions, speeds, and angles — without considering the forces that cause it.
IMU: a sensor chip combining a gyroscope and an accelerometer (sometimes a compass) to measure rotation and acceleration.
Combining readings from several imperfect sensors so each covers the others’ weaknesses, producing a better estimate than any one alone.
An algorithm that keeps a best estimate and its uncertainty, predicting with a model and correcting with measurements weighted by how much each is trusted.
Machine learning where an agent learns which actions to take by trial and error, guided only by rewards and penalties.
In Q-learning, a learned score for how much total future reward an agent expects from taking a given action in a given state.
Art that uses video and television (screens, cameras, recorded or live signals) as its material, instead of paint or stone.
A 1960s international group of artists, composers, and performers who staged playful, rule-breaking events and treated everyday actions as art.
The glass picture tube in old TVs. It fires a beam of electrons at a glowing screen, sweeping it line by line to draw the picture.
A narrow stream of electrons. Because electrons carry charge, a magnet near the beam pushes it sideways and bends the picture.
A camera wired straight to a screen nearby, so the screen shows what the camera sees right now, with no broadcast in between.
Art made by tearing, peeling, or removing layers instead of gluing them on, such as a ripped poster that shows older posters underneath.
Art built to fill a whole room or space, so viewers walk around or through it instead of looking at one object on a wall.
A machine that colors, mixes, and distorts a video signal live, the way a music synthesizer shapes sound.
A worldwide community of programmers, artists, and musicians who make real-time computer animations called demos, just to show off skill and creativity.
A festival where demosceners bring their computers, finish their demos on site, and show them on a big screen in competitions voted on by the crowd.
A plain text file released with a demo or other scene production, listing its title, authors, credits, requirements, and greetings to other groups. The name is short for "info."
A short animated intro that 1980s software crackers added to copied games to sign their work. Demos grew out of these.
A demo whose whole program must fit under a strict file size, such as 64 KB or just 4 KB, including all its graphics and music.
Making images, sounds, or worlds from math and rules while the program runs, instead of storing them as finished files.
The craft of writing a program in as few bytes as possible, squeezing every trick out of the code.
The part of a robot that notices something about the world, such as distance, light, touch, or tilt, and turns it into an electrical signal the controller can read.
A tiny computer on a single chip that reads inputs, runs one program over and over, and switches outputs. The brain of an Arduino.
The part of a machine that turns a control signal into action in the physical world, such as a motor, servo, speaker, or LED.
A cycle where a system measures the result of what it just did and uses that measurement to decide what to do next, then repeats.
A robot that runs its own sense, think, act loop without a person making each decision.
An accidental path that lets current skip the parts of a circuit and rush straight from + to −, which can make wires hot and damage boards or batteries.
An electronic part, like an LED or some capacitors, that only works when connected the right way around, with its + lead toward positive.
A reusable plastic board with metal clips inside its holes, so you can build and change circuits by pushing wires in, with no soldering.
Having a physical body that acts in the real world. A robot is embodied; a program that only changes information on a screen is not.
Control that acts without checking the result, like a toaster that heats for a set time no matter how dark the toast gets.
A drawing of a circuit that uses standard symbols to show what connects to what, not where the parts physically sit.
The 0-volt reference node of a circuit. Every voltage is measured from it, and every current path returns to it.
The letter-and-number name of a part on a schematic, like R1, C3, or U2. The same name appears on the circuit board and the parts list.
A filled dot where wires meet on a schematic, showing that they are electrically joined. Crossing wires with no dot are not connected.
A name attached to a schematic wire. Every wire with the same name is the same connection, even with no line drawn between them.
A marked spot in a circuit where you touch a meter probe to check that the voltage matches what the schematic predicts.
An unbroken conducting path between two points. A continuity test checks, with the power off, whether a wire or joint actually connects.
The terminal where conventional current leaves a diode or LED. On the symbol it is the bar; on a real LED it is the short leg beside the flat edge.
A board of pins in staggered rows that balls fall through, bouncing left or right at each row. Invented by Francis Galton to show that many random bounces pile up into a bell curve.
Five points arranged like the five on a die: four corners and one in the middle. Galton used the word for his board because its pins are staggered in this pattern.
The everyday name for the shape of a normal distribution: high in the middle, sloping down evenly on both sides.
A symmetric, bell-shaped pattern where most values sit near the mean and fewer appear farther away. About 68% of values fall within one standard deviation of the mean.
The rule that when you add up many independent random pieces, the total tends to form a bell curve, even when the pieces themselves are not bell-shaped.
Events where the outcome of one does not change the chances of the other. A ball's bounce at one pin does not depend on its bounce at the pin before.
The sunlight zone: the top ~200 m of the open ocean, where there is enough light for photosynthesis.
The twilight zone, about 200–1,000 m deep: faint blue light remains, but too little for photosynthesis.
The midnight zone, about 1,000–4,000 m deep: no sunlight at all; the only light comes from living things.
The abyssal zone, about 4,000–6,000 m deep: near-freezing, completely dark water above the vast abyssal plains.
Ocean deeper than about 6,000 m, found only inside deep-sea trenches. Named after Hades, the Greek underworld.
The upper layer of a body of water that gets enough sunlight for photosynthesis — roughly down to where 1% of surface light remains.
Pressure caused by the weight of the fluid above. In seawater it rises by about 1 atmosphere for every 10 m of depth.
At a constant temperature, a gas’s volume shrinks as its pressure rises: double the pressure, half the volume.
Trimethylamine N-oxide, a small molecule deep-sea animals store to help their proteins keep working under high pressure. It also gives fish their “fishy” smell.
A layer of water where temperature drops quickly with depth, separating warm surface water from the cold deep ocean.
Clumps of dead plankton, fecal pellets, mucus, and other organic bits that drift down from the surface and feed the deep sea.
The daily trip many sea animals make — rising toward the surface to feed at night and sinking back to deep, dark water by day. By mass, it is the largest migration on Earth.
The process that moves carbon from the ocean surface into the deep sea as sinking particles and migrating animals, keeping it out of the atmosphere.
Making food from chemical energy (such as hydrogen sulfide from vents) instead of sunlight. Microbes at hydrothermal vents and cold seeps do this.
Light made by living things through a chemical reaction, usually involving a molecule called luciferin. Common in the deep sea.
Camouflage in which an animal glows on its underside to match the faint light from above, hiding its silhouette from predators below.
The bending of light as it passes from one material into another, such as from air into water, because light changes speed.
Light bouncing off the inside surface of a material, like a ray reflecting off the back wall of a raindrop.
How many times slower light travels in a material than in a vacuum. Water is about 1.33; a higher index means more bending.
The splitting of white light into colors because each color (wavelength) refracts by a slightly different amount.
The exit angle where rays from a wide band of a raindrop bunch together. Light piles up there, making the bright bow about 42° from the antisolar point.
The point in the sky directly opposite the Sun from the viewer, marked by the shadow of the viewer's head. Rainbows are circles centered on it.
The darker strip of sky between the primary and secondary rainbows, where no once- or twice-reflected sunlight can leave the drops toward the viewer.
A faint pastel band just inside a rainbow's violet edge, caused by interference between light waves taking slightly different paths through the drop.
A broad, nearly white rainbow made by tiny fog droplets. The drops are so small that each color spreads across several degrees, and the overlapping colors blend into white.
What happens when two waves overlap: where crests meet crests they add up and get stronger, and where crests meet troughs they cancel out.
A vast, nearly empty region between the walls and filaments of the cosmic web, usually 30 to 300 million light-years across, holding only about 10–20% of the universe's average density.
The foam-like large-scale structure of the universe: galaxy clusters joined by filaments and walls, surrounding enormous empty voids.
A thread of galaxies and dark matter hundreds of millions of light-years long that connects galaxy clusters in the cosmic web.
An exceptionally large cosmic void, hundreds of millions to billions of light-years across, such as the Boötes Void or the Giant Void.
A huge collection of galaxy groups and clusters, such as our home Laniakea Supercluster, which holds about 100,000 galaxies.
A sky survey that measures the redshift, and so the distance, of many galaxies to build a 3-D map of the universe.
A region with less matter than the cosmic average. Cosmic voids are underdensities that keep emptying as the universe ages.
A galaxy that lives inside a cosmic void. Void galaxies tend to be small, blue, gas-rich, and still forming stars because they have few neighbours.
A cavity about 1,000 light-years across in the Milky Way's interstellar gas, blown out by supernovae over the last 10–20 million years. The Sun lies inside it.
The unsolved mismatch between the expansion rate of the universe measured from nearby galaxies (about 73 km/s per megaparsec) and the rate predicted from the early universe (about 67–68).
A small change in the energy of cosmic microwave background light as it crosses a void or cluster whose gravity is changing, which makes voids leave faint cold spots.
A galaxy's motion through space on top of the overall expansion of the universe, caused by the pull of nearby matter and the absence of matter in voids.
Yakov Zel'dovich's 1970 model of structure formation, in which each bit of matter keeps moving in the direction gravity first pushed it. It predicts sheets, filaments, and voids.
The distance light travels in one year, about 9.46 trillion kilometres. It is a unit of distance, not of time.
The tool at the end of a robot arm that does the work, such as a gripper, suction cup, welding torch, or paint sprayer.
The number of independent ways a mechanism can move. Each robot joint adds one; placing a tool at any position and angle in 3-D space takes six.
The space of every possible pose of a robot, such as every combination of its joint angles. In it the whole robot is a single point, so motion planning becomes moving a point around obstacle regions.
How far something sits from the camera or into the screen. In 3D software it is the Z direction, front to back.
One building block in a node editor or scene tree. Each node does one job, and you connect nodes to pass data, shapes, or behaviour from one to the next.
A point on a standing wave or vibrating surface that stays still while the parts around it move.
A picture of how two quantities are related, with one quantity on each axis and points or a line showing their values.
A named, reusable block of code. You call it by name, it can take inputs (arguments), and it can hand back a result.
The job a part does. The function of a structure in a living thing, a machine, or a design is what it is for and how it helps the whole work.
The points, edges, and faces that make up the shape of a 3D model, as opposed to its colours and materials.
When parts of a 3D scene disappear because they are closer or farther than the camera can draw, or when one object passes through another.
In mathematics, a statement that is believed to be true but has not yet been proved. The Riemann hypothesis is the most famous unsolved one.
A text window where you type commands for the computer to run, such as starting a server, installing a package, or using Git.
In a game engine or 3D program, the whole set of objects, lights, and cameras that make up one level, room, or shot.
The average distance from Earth to the Sun, about 150 million kilometres. Astronomers use it to measure distances inside the solar system.
The distance light travels in one day, about 25.9 billion kilometres or 173 astronomical units. Like a light-year, it measures distance, not time.
The scattering of light by particles much smaller than its wavelength, such as air molecules. Blue light scatters far more than red, which is why the sky and Earth from space look blue.
Streaks or rings of light caused when bright light, like the Sun, bounces around inside a camera's optics. The flare is in the camera, not in the scene.
A wide ring of icy bodies beyond Neptune, about 30 to 50 AU from the Sun. Pluto is one of its largest members.

The oldest light we can see, given off about 380,000 years after the Big Bang and stretched by expanding space into faint microwaves. It comes from every direction and marks the edge of the observable universe.
The boundary where the Sun's outflowing solar wind is stopped by the gas between the stars. Crossing it means entering interstellar space. Voyager 1 crossed it in August 2012.
The space between the stars, beyond the heliopause, where the thin gas comes from other stars rather than from the Sun.
The part of the universe whose light has had time to reach us since the Big Bang. It is about 93 billion light-years across because space expanded while the light travelled.

In England, a Protestant Christian who worshipped outside the official Church of England, such as a Baptist, Quaker, Methodist, or Moravian. Dissenters faced legal limits on schooling and public office until the 1800s.

A Protestant church with roots in 1400s Bohemia and Moravia, renewed in Germany in 1722. Moravians stressed a warm, personal love for Jesus, hymn singing, and simple community life, and they had a congregation in London in Blake's time.

The belief that grace and love, not obedience to moral rules, are what make a person right with God. Opponents use it as a charge of lawlessness; readers often use it to describe Blake's attacks on rule-based religion.

A school in 1700s Britain paid for by church donations to teach poor children reading, religion, and a trade. Pupils wore uniforms in their school's colors and were marched to public services to show donors their charity at work.
A minor church or parish officer who kept order at services and processions, often carrying a staff of office. In Blake's Holy Thursday the beadles lead the charity children into St Paul's.

Blake's name for his books in which the words and pictures were etched together on copper, printed, and colored by hand. The term borrows from medieval illuminated manuscripts of the Bible and prayer books.

The Frankfurt School's approach to studying society. Instead of only describing how things are, it asks who benefits, what is hidden, and how people could be freer. Named in Max Horkheimer's 1937 essay "Traditional and Critical Theory."
The thinkers connected with the Institute for Social Research, founded in Frankfurt, Germany, in 1923, including Max Horkheimer, Theodor W. Adorno, Herbert Marcuse, and later Jürgen Habermas.

German philosopher, sociologist, and composer (1903–1969), a leading member of the Frankfurt School. With Max Horkheimer he wrote Dialectic of Enlightenment, which includes the chapter "The Culture Industry."
Adorno and Horkheimer's name for film, radio, music, and magazines produced like factory goods by large companies. They argued it standardizes taste and trains people to conform while feeling free.
In Adorno's sense, making songs, films, and shows from the same formulas so every product is interchangeable and nothing truly surprises the audience.
Adorno's term for small surface differences, like a star's hairstyle or a catchphrase, that make standardized products seem unique and let buyers feel they are expressing themselves.
Karl Marx's idea, used by Adorno, that people treat the price or market value of a thing as if it were its real worth, for example valuing a concert for the cost of the ticket rather than the music.

Walter Benjamin's word for the sense of presence and authority a unique original artwork has in its own time and place. He argued photography and film strip art of its aura, which could make art more democratic.
A mathematical tool that takes a signal (like a sound wave) and finds which frequencies are in it and how strong each one is, turning a waveform into a spectrum.
A shortcut way of computing the Fourier transform (Cooley and Tukey, 1965) that is fast enough for computers to analyse sound, radio and images in real time.
Describing a signal by how it changes over time — the waveform you would see on an oscilloscope, with amplitude on one axis and time on the other.
Describing a signal by which frequencies it contains and how strong each is — the spectrum, with amplitude on one axis and frequency on the other.
A chart of a signal’s ingredients: each frequency it contains and how much of it there is.
A sine-wave component of a sound at a whole-number multiple (2×, 3×, 4×…) of the fundamental frequency. The mix of harmonics gives an instrument its timbre.
The lowest frequency in a musical sound — the rate at which the whole wave pattern repeats. It sets the pitch you hear.
The "colour" or character of a sound that lets you tell a flute from a violin playing the same note at the same loudness. It comes from the mix of harmonics.
How many measurements (samples) per second a digital system takes of a signal. CD audio uses 44,100 samples per second.
Half the sampling rate — the highest frequency a sampled system can capture correctly. Anything above it gets aliased.
When a frequency above the Nyquist limit is sampled too slowly and shows up as a fake, lower frequency — like wagon wheels that seem to spin backward on film.
A set of audio filters that boost or cut chosen bands of frequencies, used to shape the tone of music or remove unwanted sounds like hum.
A logarithmic unit for comparing loudness or signal strength. Every +6 dB roughly doubles a wave’s amplitude; every +10 dB is about ten times the power.
The height of a wave — how far it swings from its resting middle line. For sound, bigger amplitude means louder.
How many bits are used to store each sample of a digital signal. More bits give more levels to round to, so less quantization noise: 16-bit audio has 65,536 levels.
Rounding each measured sample to the nearest allowed level when a signal is digitised. The rounding errors are heard as a faint hiss called quantization noise.
A chip that measures a continuously changing voltage (like a microphone signal) many times a second and turns each measurement into a number a computer can store.
A filter that lets frequencies above its cutoff through and turns down everything below it. Used to remove rumble and hum.
A filter that lets frequencies below its cutoff through and turns down everything above it. Used to remove hiss and to stop aliasing before sampling.
A filter that removes one narrow band of frequencies, such as 60 Hz electrical hum, while leaving the rest of the sound almost untouched.
The angle between a planet's spin axis and a line straight up from its orbit. Earth's is about 23.4°, and it is the cause of the seasons.
One of two moments each year (about June 21 and December 21) when one hemisphere leans most toward the Sun, giving it the longest day, and the other has its shortest day.
One of two moments each year (about March 20 and September 22) when the Sun is straight over the Equator and day and night are nearly equal everywhere.
The slow wobble of Earth's axis, like a spinning top, that traces a circle in the sky about every 26,000 years and changes which star is the pole star.
The point in an orbit where a planet is closest to the Sun. Earth reaches it around January 3, at about 147.1 million km.
The point in an orbit where a planet is farthest from the Sun. Earth reaches it around July 4, at about 152.1 million km.
The spot on Earth where the Sun is straight overhead. It moves between the Tropic of Cancer and the Tropic of Capricorn over the year.
The latitude lines at 23.4°N (Cancer) and 23.4°S (Capricorn): the farthest north and south the Sun is ever straight overhead. Their latitude equals Earth's tilt.
The latitude line at about 66.6°N (66.6°S for the Antarctic Circle). Beyond it there is at least one day of 24-hour sun and one of 24-hour night each year.
Incoming solar radiation: how much sunlight energy reaches a surface, measured in watts per square meter (W/m²).
Slow cycles in Earth's tilt, wobble (precession), and orbit shape, lasting tens of thousands of years, that shift sunlight across the globe and help pace the ice ages.
A bright star close to the point in the sky where Earth's axis points. Today it is Polaris; precession slowly changes it over thousands of years.
Blender's main editor: the window where you see, select, and change objects in 3D space.
Blender's mode for arranging whole objects: moving, rotating, scaling, adding, and deleting them.
Blender's mode for reshaping one mesh by selecting and moving its vertices, edges, and faces. Tab switches in and out.
Blender's list of every object and collection in the file. Click a row to select it; double-click to rename it.
Blender's tabbed settings panel for the active object and scene: modifiers, materials, render settings, and more.
The panel on the right of Blender's 3D Viewport (N toggles it). Its Item tab shows exact Location, Rotation, Scale, and Dimensions.
The red-and-white target in Blender's viewport that marks where new objects appear. Shift+S moves it; Shift+right-click places it.
The colored arrows, rings, or handles drawn on a selected object for moving, rotating, or scaling it by dragging. Red is X, green is Y, blue is Z.
A view with no perspective shrinking: parallel edges stay parallel, so sizes can be compared and measured. Blender's Front, Right, and Top views use it.
A Blender modifier that combines two meshes: Difference cuts one out of the other, Union joins them, Intersect keeps only the overlap.
A mesh used only to carve volume out of another mesh through a Boolean modifier. Hide it rather than deleting it so the cut stays editable.
A closed, watertight mesh with a clear inside and outside. Booleans and 3D printing both depend on it.
A non-destructive operation stacked on a 3D object, like Bevel or Mirror. It stays editable until you apply it into the real mesh.
One of the thin bars that divide a window into separate panes of glass.
The direction a mesh face points outward. Flipped normals make faces shade dark or wrong; Shift+N recalculates them in Blender.
Building a 3D model by reshaping a simple primitive, usually a cube, with extrudes, insets, and loop cuts.
A Blender modifier that reflects a mesh across its origin's axis, so you model one half and get a symmetrical whole.
The orange dot that is a 3D object's own pivot point. It sets where Location is measured and what the object rotates and mirrors around.
Blender's way of shading curved areas smoothly while keeping edges sharper than a chosen angle crisp.
What you see after a Blender object's modifiers run, which can differ from the mesh you actually edit underneath.
A named folder of objects in Blender's Outliner. Collections organize a scene and can be appended into other files.
Linking 3D objects so that moving, rotating, or scaling the parent carries its children along (Ctrl+P in Blender).
A small set of 3D pieces built to one grid size, like walls, floors, and doorways, that snap together into many different layouts.
Blender snapping that moves objects in fixed grid steps, so modular pieces line up exactly.
A copy that shares mesh data with its source (Alt+D in Blender). Edit the shape of one and every linked copy updates.
A quick gray pass of simple shapes that tests scale, layout, and composition before any detail or texture work.
How a 3D mesh's vertices, edges, and faces are arranged and flow across its surface. Clean topology bends well when animated.
A four-sided mesh face. Quads subdivide smoothly and form clean edge loops, so they are the standard for characters.
A vertex where 3, or 5 or more, edges meet instead of the usual 4. Poles are needed but can pinch subdivided surfaces.
A mesh face with five or more sides. Fine on flat surfaces, but it can shade and subdivide badly on curves.
Blender's Edit Mode tool (K) that cuts new edges across faces wherever you click.
A Blender toggle (O) that also moves nearby geometry with a smooth falloff. A circle around the pointer means it's on.
A Blender modifier that splits every face into smaller ones and smooths the result, turning a low-poly cage into a rounded form.
A value on a mesh edge that makes Subdivision Surface keep that edge sharper instead of rounding it off.
A Blender modifier that recalculates shading based on face size, removing dark pinches around bevels on hard-surface models.
A Blender modifier that gives a flat surface real thickness, like turning a sheet into a wall.
Modeling rigid, manufactured things such as tools, vehicles, and buildings, with crisp edges and precise cuts.
A flat 2D layout of a 3D mesh's surface, like a cardboard box unfolded, that tells a texture image where to land.
An edge marked so the UV unwrap splits the mesh open there, like the seams of a sewing pattern.
Blender's all-in-one material node. Its sliders, like Base Color, Roughness, and Metallic, follow real physics.
Blender's mode for painting color with a brush straight onto a model's image texture.
A named set of mesh vertices, each with a weight from 0 to 1, used by modifiers, shaders, and armatures.
A Blender shader node that reads a named mesh value, like a vertex group, into the material.
A Blender node that remaps values through a gradient you shape with draggable color stops.
A Blender viewport toggle that makes the scene camera follow every orbit, pan, and zoom, so you can frame a shot by navigating.
Blender's fast, real-time render engine, built on the same graphics techniques as video games.
Blender's path-traced render engine. It is slower than EEVEE, but its light bounces and shadows are physically accurate.
Blender's mode for pushing, pulling, and smoothing a dense mesh with brushes, like digital clay.
Dynamic Topology: a Blender sculpting option that adds mesh detail only where the brush touches.
Rebuilds a sculpted mesh with evenly sized faces at one chosen resolution, cleaning up stretched areas.
A painted area of a mesh that sculpting brushes leave alone, protecting it while you work nearby.
A named, colored region of a sculpted mesh used to hide, mask, or select that region quickly.
Blender's node-based system for building and changing geometry procedurally, like scattering trees or rocks by rules instead of by hand.
In Geometry Nodes, a value worked out separately for every point or face, such as each point's height.
A Geometry Nodes node that scatters points across a mesh's surface, often the first step in scattering objects.
A Geometry Nodes node that places a lightweight copy of an object at every point, without duplicating its mesh.
Blender's node editor for adjusting a finished render, with glow, color, blur, and layering, before the image is saved.
The Compositor's input node. It carries the rendered image and its separate passes into the node graph.
The Compositor's output node. Whatever reaches it is the final image Blender saves.
A Compositor node for previewing any point in the graph without changing the saved render.
A Compositor node that adds bloom, streaks, or a glow around the brightest parts of a render.
HyperText Markup Language: the tags that say what each part of a web page is — a heading, a list, a link, an image.
Cascading Style Sheets: the rules that decide how HTML looks — colour, spacing, type and layout.
The programming language browsers run, used to make a page respond: clicks, typing, searching, animation and games.

One piece of a page: an opening tag, its content, and a closing tag, such as

A paragraph.

. The tag name says what the piece is.
A setting written inside an opening tag as name="value", such as href on a link or alt on an image. It configures that one element.
Choosing the element that matches what content is — <nav> for navigation, <button> for an action — instead of a meaningless <div>, so browsers and assistive technology understand the page.
A major region of a page — header, nav, main or footer — that screen reader users can jump to directly.
The words in an image’s alt attribute, read aloud or shown in place of the picture. Write what the image communicates; use alt="" for pure decoration.
Directions to a file that start from the folder of the page you are writing in, such as images/logo.svg or ../index.html. They keep working when the whole folder moves to a server.
A file address that starts from a fixed top — the root of a domain (/style.css) or a drive (C:\…). Drive paths only work on one computer.
The first part of a CSS rule, which picks the elements the rule applies to — h1, .card, #intro or nav a.
How CSS decides which rule wins when two disagree: an id beats a class, a class beats an element name, and a tie goes to the rule written later.
The idea that every element is a rectangle made of content, then padding, then a border, then margin — the four layers you size and space with CSS.
A CSS layout mode that lines items up in one row or one column and shares out the spare space between them.
A CSS layout mode that places items into rows and columns at the same time — ideal for a page of cards.
A CSS condition, such as @media (min-width: 700px), that applies rules only when the screen or device matches it.
Building one page whose layout adapts to any screen width, from a phone to a projector, instead of a separate site for each.
A number comparing the lightness of text and its background. WCAG asks for at least 4.5 : 1 for normal text so more people can read it.
Document Object Model: the live tree of objects the browser builds from your HTML, which JavaScript reads and changes.
A function you attach to an element with addEventListener, which runs when something happens there — a click, a key press, typing.
The developer tools built into every browser (F12): the Console shows messages and errors, Network shows every file requested, Elements shows the live page.
A small web server running on your own computer, such as Live Server, so your site is fetched over http://localhost the way a real host serves it.
The HTTP status a server sends when nothing exists at the requested address. In DevTools it names the exact file the browser could not find.
A saved snapshot of every file in a Git project at one moment, with your name, the time and a message saying why it changed.
A project folder tracked by Git, including its full history of commits. On GitHub it is the online copy you push to.
A free GitHub service that serves the files in a repository as a public website, exactly as they are, with no code running on the server.
Separately installed software that ran inside a web page to add abilities the browser lacked, such as Flash Player. Modern browsers no longer run them.
Adobe’s browser plugin that played animations and games from .swf files for over twenty years. Adobe ended support on 31 December 2020.
Software that imitates an older system so its files can run on modern machines — Ruffle, for example, plays Flash content without the plugin.
The time since the last frame of an animation loop. Multiplying movement by it keeps speed the same on fast and slow screens.
The browser standard for virtual and augmented reality, letting a web page draw a 3D scene in a supported headset.
A keyboard instrument whose strings are plucked by small quills when you press the keys. It is bright and clear, but every note sounds at the same loudness however you press.
An early keyboard instrument in which each key presses a small brass blade (a tangent) against a string. Touch changes its loudness, but it is very quiet.
The early piano of the 1700s and early 1800s, with a wooden frame, leather-covered hammers, and a lighter sound than a modern piano. Its name means “loud-soft.”
In a piano, the part of the action that lets the hammer fly free and fall back the instant it strikes the string, so the string can keep ringing.
Laying a piano's long bass strings diagonally over the other strings, so they fit in the case and drive the middle of the soundboard.
A large, thin wooden board in a piano or other string instrument that picks up the strings' vibrations and moves the air, making them loud enough to hear.
A round-backed, short-necked string instrument with no frets, played across the Middle East and North Africa. Brought to Spain in the Middle Ages, it became the ancestor of the European lute.
A guitar-shaped Spanish instrument of the 1500s with six pairs of strings, tuned like a lute and used for solo music.
A pair (sometimes a trio) of strings tuned together and played as if they were one string, as on early guitars, lutes, and today's 12-string guitar.
Thin wooden strips glued under a classical guitar's top in a fan shape, keeping the top strong while leaving it free to vibrate.
An acoustic guitar with thin metal cones inside that act like loudspeakers, making it louder and brighter than a wooden guitar. Invented in the 1920s.
A magnet wrapped in thousands of turns of copper wire. A vibrating steel string disturbs its magnetic field and makes a small electric signal that an amplifier can make loud.
An electric guitar with a solid wooden body instead of a hollow one, so it can be played very loud without howling feedback.
A page of music with just the melody on one staff and chord symbols above it; each player makes up their own part from the chords.
A collection of lead sheets. Musicians “fake” (make up) the accompaniment from the chord symbols instead of reading every note.
A short name written above the melody, like G7 or Am, that tells the band which chord to play until the next symbol.
One or more notes before the first full bar of a tune, leading into the first strong beat. Also called an anacrusis.
An instrument whose written notes are not the notes that sound. On a B♭ trumpet, a written C sounds as B♭, so its music is written a step higher.
The notes as they actually sound, the way a piano plays them. Parts for transposing instruments are written in a different key from concert pitch.
Turning a melody upside down: every move up becomes the same-sized move down, mirrored around a starting note.
In music, playing a melody backwards, from its last note to its first.
A chord with a note other than the root on the bottom. First inversion puts the 3rd on the bottom; second inversion puts the 5th there.
How a chord’s notes are arranged: which one is on the bottom, how far apart they are, and which are doubled or left out.
Moving from one chord to the next so that each note, or voice, travels as short a distance as possible.
A three-note chord of just the root, 3rd and 7th: the notes that tell you what kind of chord it is. A favorite of bebop pianists.
Playing pairs of eighth notes long-short (roughly two-to-one) instead of evenly. The basic rhythm of jazz.
Putting notes or accents off the beat, so the music pushes against the steady pulse.
A jazz bass line with a note on every beat that steps through the chord and leads into the next chord.
Short for accompanying: a pianist or guitarist playing chords in rhythm behind a melody or a soloist.
Taking turns improvising four bars at a time with another player, often the drummer.
A 12-bar chord pattern: four bars of the I chord, two of IV, two of I, then V, IV, I and often V. The backbone of the blues, early rock and roll and much jazz.
Creative works whose copyright has run out (or never existed). Anyone may copy, perform and change them.
Controlling a robot or machine from a distance, with a person deciding each move while watching through cameras or sensors.
How many signal symbols a serial link sends per second. At 9600 baud with 10 bits per byte, about 960 bytes travel each second.
terms.etymology: Named after Émile Baudot, inventor of an early telegraph code.

terms.definition: PWM: switching power on and off very fast and changing how long it stays on, so a digital pin can make a motor run slow, medium, or fast.
A motor with a built-in position sensor and controller that turns to an exact angle you ask for and holds it there.
terms.etymology: Latin servus “servant”: it obeys a command signal.

terms.definition: A sensor that sends out a sound too high for people to hear and times the echo to measure how far away an object is.
BLE: a short-range radio standard that sends small packets of data using very little power. Web pages can talk to BLE devices through Web Bluetooth.
terms.etymology: Bluetooth is named after Harald “Bluetooth” Gormsson, a Danish king who united tribes, as the standard unites devices.

terms.definition: An agreed set of rules for how two devices format, send, and answer messages, so each side understands the other.
terms.etymology: Greek prōtokollon, the first sheet glued to a scroll describing its contents.

terms.definition: JavaScript Object Notation: a plain-text format for data written as names and values in curly braces, like {"N":3,"D2":150}.
A safety control that stops a machine automatically unless the operator keeps actively holding it or keeps sending signals.
terms.etymology: From train controls that stop the train if the driver collapses and lets go.

terms.definition: A small message sent on a regular schedule just to prove a connection is still alive. When the heartbeats stop, the other side assumes something went wrong.
A connection that lets a web page and a server send messages back and forth instantly, as long as the page is open.
How many degrees a twisted shape turns for every millimetre it rises. On a spiral cone fidget it is also how far the cone spins for each millimetre it drops.
A Blender modifier that twists, bends, tapers, or stretches a whole mesh. In Twist mode it turns each slice of the mesh in proportion to its height.
